chapter: Names, influences and early blues singers
title: Ma Rainey, Mamie Smith and New Orleans blues singers
summary: She worked on the same dates as Ma Rainey and heard the Smiths. She calls Mamie Smith's Crazy Blues the first popular blues record, and mentions Tilly Johnson and Ann Cook.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: Of these, did you hear any of the big famous blues singers when you're down here, people like Ma Rainey or Bessie Smith?

Oh, yeah, I worked with Ma Rainey, like we played what you call day and date, you know. I was sure maybe, I was sure in one theater, her show in another theater like that, you know, see. Sure, I heard Ma Rainey, in fact, I heard them all, Bessie Smith, Clara Smith, Mamie Smith, you know. Who of them did you like the best? Well, when I first heard the first record of Mamie Smith, the Crazy Blues, I liked it fine, you know. Yeah, and I liked her style, I liked her way of singing. That was the first blues record in the late, yeah, late. But they had been, they claimed that they had been, I did know her, I knew her, but I'd forgotten her name. Now, I think, no, it wasn't, it wasn't, it wasn't O'Vara Johnson, who had went to Europe with this white performer that taken, she was the first one that went to Europe and taken colored performers with her. Well, they claimed they had made a record a long time ago on the Victor, you know, singing blues, but it was never, I don't think, you know, made popular like Mamie Smith. I think Mamie Smith is the first real popular blues singer, Mamie Smith. She sang that Crazy Blues.
Well, who were some of the singers around town that were prominent on the order of Ma Rainey? You mean here in New Orleans? In New Orleans, did you hear her?

Her name was, oh, she was Dad James' wife. Dad James was a sort of a producer and a comedian that gave shows around. Tilly Johnson, Tilly Johnson. She was, I think, one of the, you know, another, what I call, coon shouter, too, you know.
Ann Cook singing when you were coming out?
Oh, well, no, Ann Cook, that's before my time. That was before my time. Though I've met Ann Cook and she's told me about her, you know, her singing, but I never heard her sing.
